passage: Tuesday Dear Diary, Ishita didn't play dog-and-bone again. When the whistle went she walked to the far bench with her hands over her ears. Priyal said she's snobby. I don't think so. At lunch Ishita told me the whole route of the night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping. I didn't understand half, but her eyes went shiny. So today I asked her, "Do you want to play something, or is the bench better?" She said, "Can we play trains?" We drew a timetable game in chalk. I was the passenger, she was the station master. Three more girls joined. Ishita laughed so loud! Tomorrow she's bringing her train cards. - Kavitha

qa.q: Which train's route did Ishita describe at lunch?
qa.a: The night train to Guwahati, every station, without stopping.

qa.q: What does Kavitha think about Priyal calling Ishita snobby?
qa.a: Kavitha doesn't agree and seems to think Ishita avoids the game for another reason, like the noise, not because she is proud.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha opened up a real friendship?
qa.a: Kavitha asked Ishita what she wanted instead of assuming, then played a train game built around Ishita's interest.

qa.q: How might Ishita see break time differently after the chalk timetable game?
qa.a: Break may feel like a place where she belongs, since others joined a game she loves and she laughed out loud.

grounding: A classmate notices a peer who avoids loud games and talks a lot about trains, asks instead of assuming, and includes her through her interest.

passage: During games period at the government school, some boys yelled "Train-wali!" as Pallavi slipped away from the noisy kabaddi circle. The new girl, Lalremsiami, watched her sit under the neem tree, counting on her fingers: engine, eleven wagons, guard van. Instead of guessing, Lalremsiami sat down a little distance away. "Do you want company, or quiet?" Pallavi thought. "Company. But no shouting." "Which train comes past here at four?" Pallavi's whole face opened. She explained the goods train with cement wagons and why it always waits at the signal. After school they stood at the level crossing and counted the wagons out loud together. Next day, when someone called "Train-wali" again, Lalremsiami said, "She knows more than the stationmaster," and kept walking beside her.

qa.q: What was Pallavi counting on her fingers under the neem tree?
qa.a: Engine, eleven wagons, guard van.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami seem to feel about Pallavi, and how can you tell she did not want to assume what Pallavi needed?
qa.a: She seemed curious and caring; she sat a little distance away and asked, 'Do you want company, or quiet?' instead of guessing.

qa.q: What turning point changed the teasing on the second day?
qa.a: Lalremsiami refused to join in, answered the teasing calmly and kept walking beside Pallavi.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when Lalremsiami asks about the four o'clock train?
qa.a: Pallavi likely felt seen and happy; her whole face opened, and she gladly explained the goods train.

grounding: A classmate notices a girl who avoids loud games and talks about trains, asks instead of assuming, does not tease and builds friendship around her interest.

passage: At recess in a Madrid school yard, the dodgeball game got louder and louder. Mateo noticed Omar walk to the far wall again, hands over his ears. Omar had told him all about night trains once, for nearly half an hour. Some boys called Omar "train boy." Mateo almost joined in, then went over instead. "Do you not like dodgeball, or do you not like the noise?" Omar thought. "The noise." Mateo pulled chalk from his pocket. "Can you draw the night train route?" Soon a chalk railway stretched along the wall, and two younger kids were asking which stop came next.

qa.q: Where did Omar walk when the dodgeball game got loud?
qa.a: He walked to the far wall, hands over his ears.

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when he almost joined the teasing?
qa.a: He felt tempted and a little unsure, but he was curious about Omar and chose to go and ask instead.

qa.q: Why was asking Omar a good choice?
qa.a: Mateo found out the problem was the noise, not the game, so he could offer something that fitted what Omar liked.

qa.q: What might the chalk railway mean to Omar?
qa.a: Omar may feel included and understood, because his favourite subject became something others wanted to join.

grounding: Shows a classmate who notices someone avoiding loud games and loving trains, and builds friendship by asking and including rather than teasing.

passage: At the summer camp in the community hall, the counsellor announced musical chairs with the speaker on full. Yash backed into the corner, pressing his fists to his ears. Madhuri had heard him explain every metro line in the city twice that week. A boy near her snorted. "He's so weird." Madhuri shook her head. "Don't." She walked to Yash and waited, not too close. "Is it the music?" He nodded without looking at her. "Want to make a metro quiz for the others instead?" His hands came down. By snack time six children were shouting station names, and Yash was keeping score, smiling at the chart.

qa.q: How many children were shouting station names by snack time?
qa.a: By snack time six children were shouting station names.

qa.q: How did Madhuri probably feel when the boy called Yash weird?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable and protective, because she told the boy "Don't" and went to check on Yash.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that helped Yash join in?
qa.a: She stood at a respectful distance, asked what the problem was and suggested a metro quiz built on his interest.

qa.q: What might the camp feel like for Yash after the quiz?
qa.a: Yash may feel accepted and proud, keeping score in a game about something he loves instead of hiding in the corner.

grounding: Shows a peer noticing a classmate who avoids loud games and loves trains, and including him by asking rather than assuming.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I'm in Omkar's class. On sports day, when the drums started for the relay, Omkar went and sat under the gulmohar tree with his jumper pulled over his ears. I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Some boys shouted that he was a scaredy-cat. I didn't want to guess, so I asked him, "Do you want me to go away or stay?" He said, "Stay. Quiet." After a while he told me about the goods trains that pass his building, how many wagons each one has. I brought my train card game the next morning. We play it every lunch now, and Omkar laughs when he wins.

qa.q: Where did Omkar sit when the drums started?
qa.a: He sat under the gulmohar tree with his jumper pulled over his ears.

qa.q: What does Kashish's decision to ask rather than guess suggest about Kashish's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Kashish felt respectful and curious, and cared more about what Omkar needed than about joining the teasing.

qa.q: What small step turned the sports day moment into a friendship?
qa.a: Kashish brought a train card game the next morning, building on Omkar's interest, and they now play every lunch.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Kashish now?
qa.a: Omkar may see Kashish as a safe and trusted friend who listens and shares his love of trains.

grounding: Shows a classmate observing a peer who avoids loud events and loves trains, and building real friendship by asking and sharing his interest.

passage:
Monday. Leela noticed that Zubin never joined kho-kho. He sat on the steps, hands over his ears, and told anyone passing about the Rajdhani's engine numbers. Some boys called him Train Brain. Leela didn't laugh, but she didn't say anything either.
Thursday. Leela sat next to him. "Why don't you play?" she asked. "Too loud," Zubin said. "Trains are loud too, but I like that loud." Leela laughed. "Can you teach me the engine numbers?"
The next Monday. For the class project, Leela suggested making a railway map of India. Zubin drew every route from memory while three others coloured the stations. When Aryan said "Train Brain" again, Leela said, "He's our map expert, actually." Zubin didn't look up, but he was smiling.

qa.q: What did Leela suggest for the class project?
qa.a: A railway map of India.

qa.q: Why did Leela sit next to Zubin on Thursday?
qa.a: She was curious about him and a bit uneasy about staying silent while others teased him, so she wanted to ask rather than assume.

qa.q: What small steps helped Leela build a real friendship with Zubin?
qa.a: She asked why he didn't play, took an interest in his trains and planned a project around them, and stood up to the teasing.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when Leela calls him the map expert?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and accepted, even though he doesn't look up, because a classmate valued what he loves.

grounding: Leela notices a classmate who avoids loud games and loves trains, asks instead of assuming, includes him through his interest and stops the teasing.
